content.overview: BNS s. 40 — Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body.
content.study:
Introduction and meaning
Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body. BNS restatement of IPC 102. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 102. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.
In student language: BNS s. 40 is the rule on “Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body”. The section provides that the right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Why this is asked
Criminal law arguments turn on statutory ingredients. BNS s. 40 exists so that “Commencement and continuance of right of private defence of body” has a closed legal test in Chapter III — General Exceptions. An authoritative analysis defines the concept, lists every ingredient, walks the statutory illustrations, states exceptions, and applies the test methodically to facts.
Chapter setting: When an act is not an offence: mistake, accident, infancy, unsoundness, consent, compulsion — and the right of private defence.

The provision in detail
40. The right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues

Essential ingredients

learningObjectives: Understand the temporal duration of the right of private defence of the body under BNS s. 40.
Analyze the triggering point: commencement upon reasonable apprehension from attempt or threat.
Identify the termination point: continuance only as long as apprehension of danger continues.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 40 provides that the right of private defence of the body commences as soon as a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises from an attempt or threat to commit the offence, though the offence may not have been committed; and it continues as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The right of private defence is strictly co-extensive with the reasonable apprehension of danger. It begins the instant an overt attempt or credible threat creates reasonable fear of bodily harm, and it ceases the instant that apprehension is dispelled.
statutoryFramework: Chapter III — General Exceptions, BNS s. 40 (corresponding to IPC s. 102).
Commencement: When 'reasonable apprehension of danger to the body arises' from an attempt or threat.
Pre-emptive right: Offence 'may not have been committed' — victim does not have to wait for the first blow.
Continuance: 'as long as such apprehension of danger to the body continues'.
Termination: Right ends immediately upon disarmament, surrender, or retreat of assailant.
essentialIngredients: An attempt or threat to commit an offence against the body occurred.
The attempt or threat generated a reasonable apprehension of danger to the body.
The defensive act was committed during the subsistence of that apprehension.
The defensive act ceased once the apprehension of danger ended.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 40 answers the critical question: WHEN can self-defence begin, and WHEN must it stop? The law does not require a citizen to passively wait until a knife has slashed his arm or a bullet has grazed his cheek. As soon as an assailant draws a dagger, points a loaded gun, or lunges forward with lethal threats, the right commences immediately. Conversely, the moment the assailant is disarmed, knocked unconscious, drops his weapon, turns his back, or flees, the apprehension of danger is extinguished. Any blow struck after that moment is not defence; it is revenge, and constitutes an offence.
examples: Teaching example (Commencement): An enemy reaches into his jacket, draws a revolver, and cocks it while shouting 'I will kill you'. The victim immediately tackles the enemy and dislocates his shoulder. The right commenced as soon as the threat generated reasonable apprehension; the victim was not required to wait for a shot.

Teaching example (Cessation): An assailant lunges with a knife. The defender knocks the knife away, and the assailant falls to the ground pleading for mercy. The defender then takes a stick and repeatedly strikes the helpless assailant on the head. The right ceased the moment the knife was knocked away; the subsequent strikes are criminal assault.
distinctions: Pre-emptive defence vs Mere empty words: Mere verbal abuse without physical capability or overt gesture does not create reasonable apprehension; an overt threat or attempt is required.
Continuing threat vs Terminated threat: If the attacker retreats only to fetch a deadlier weapon, the apprehension may continue; if he flees the scene entirely, the right terminates.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who pursued a retreating attacker for fifty meters and stabbed him is protected by private defence.
Rule: BNS s. 40 provides that private defence continues only as long as apprehension of danger continues.
Application: Once the attacker turned and ran, the immediate threat to the accused's body ceased. The pursuit transformed the act from defensive preservation into retributive aggression.
Conclusion: Section 40 does not protect the accused after the threat ceased; private defence is lost.
